newsitem.title: CROATIA: Election ends revolt that broke up Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: Election ends revolt that broke up Yugoslavia.

text.p: When Serbs vote in Croatia's elections on Sunday they will be abandoning a revolt that began in 1990 when peasant gunmen rolled logs across roads at the height of the tourist season.

What scornful Croats dubbed the "Log Revolution" mushroomed into a war that broke up Yugoslavia, spawned a rebel mini-state inside Croatia shored up by U.N. peacekeepers, and set the stage for a far bloodier conflagration in nearby Bosnia.

Croatia finally turned the tables on its minority Serbs in 1995 when it recaptured more than 25 percent of the country -- all but a sliver of rebel territory -- in six days of blitz warfare that humiliated the United Nations.
The Serbs in one last small enclave, Eastern Slavonia, agreed in talks mediated by the United States to settle for minority rights and peacefully rejoin Croatia after elections.

But the end of their rebellion seemed final only last month when Serb leaders gave up manoeuvring to preserve their autonomy in other guises and agreed to vote on the day set by Croatia and the transitional U.N. administrator of the enclave.
The Serbs will join Croats in voting for municipal and county governments countrywide and hope to elect Serb majority councils in about a dozen of Eastern Slavonia's 28 districts.

That modest goal is a sobering comedown from the crusade for sovereignty within a "Greater Serbia" that erupted seven years ago after Croatian nationalists seeking independence from Yugoslavia defeated communists in free elections.

Propaganda spread by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic revived Croatian Serbs' memories of genocide at the hands of Croatia's Nazi puppet regime in World War Two, persuading them that the new Croatian government was a fascist reincarnation.

It was not. But Milosevic, bent on spoiling Croatia's pending secession, incited rural Serbs to rise up and grab strategic land for incorporation into a Greater Serbia that would replace an exhausted, multinational Yugoslavia.
Led by a pugnacious police captain, Milan Martic, Serb gunmen laid logs across roads leading to their bastion town, Knin, on a mountain plateau looming over the Adriatic coast.
Roads and railway traffic through Serb-populated regions between north and south Croatia were blocked while Western tourists frolicked on Dalmatian beaches, but not for long.
Shielded and supplied by the Yugoslav federal army (JNA), Martic whipped bearded brawlers into a credible rebel force.
Milan Babic, a cherub-faced country dentist, took over a new ultra-nationalist Serb Democratic Party (SDS) that revelled in the regalia of the old royalist "Chetnik" movement.

"Simple Serb peasants were traumatised by unscrupulous politicians wishing to realise their politics of nationalist fantasy," wrote Laura Silber and Allan Little in their book, "The Death of Yugoslavia".
In April 1991, a Croat policeman died in a shootout with Serb irregulars after they occupied Plitvice National Park, the first casualty of what became a broader Yugoslav conflict.

A month later, 12 Croat policemen trying to reassert control in the eastern town of Borovo Selo were shot dead in an ambush by Serb irregulars. Some Croat bodies were mutilated, initiating a cycle of atrocities recalling World War Two.
Full-blown war erupted after President Franjo Tudjman's government declared independence in June 1991.

Serb militia, backed by the Yugoslav federal army (JNA), overwhelmed weak Croat defenders and conquered a vast swathe of territory stretching from 30 km (18 miles) south of Zagreb almost to the Dalmatian seaboard, a wedge of central Croatia and the fertile Eastern Slavonia crescent bordering Serbia.
JNA firepower demolished the pretty Danube town of Vukovar in an infamous marathon siege and Serb forces machinegunned 260 hospital patients in the aftermath, the war's worst crime.

But the "Republic of Serb Krajina" (RSK) declared in Croatia suffered what would prove a crippling economic blow when Zagreb repulsed Serb efforts to punch through to the coast and enjoy access to maritime markets.
While government-run Croatia began to prosper with Western high-tech, Serb territory became a primitive backwater where farming, smuggling and banditry provided the only income.
Serb glory turned to gloom and despondency. Many militiamen turned to gangsterism or deserted for "normal life" abroad.

The Serbs did not rebuild war-gutted housing or even clear away wreckage. Instead they ransacked U.N. relief convoys bound for Bosnia and sporadically shelled Adriatic resorts to numb a tourist industry they could not run themselves.

When Croatian troops reconquered territory in 1995, Martic retaliated with a long-range rocket bombardment of Zagreb that killed six civilians and wounded almost 200. That earned him an indictment by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
He and Babic vanished into obscurity in Serb-held Bosnia.

But the Croatians, while triumphant in war, still suffer international opprobrium over the flight of 180,000 Serbs from the 1995 offensive. An honest effort to resettle those Serbs is a condition for Croatia's integration in Europe
